tip: The ongoing past sets the scene, the one-off past interrupts: διάβαζα (dhiávaza = I was reading) when ήρθε (írthe = came) cuts in.
Ξαφνικά (ksafniká = suddenly) is a signal word – it flips the sentence to the one-off past: χτύπησε (khtípise = it knocked), not the ongoing form.
Habit vs change: κάπνιζε (kápnize = he used to smoke), σταμάτησε (stamátise = he stopped, once).
Same verb, two pasts: άκουσα (ákusa = I heard, once), άκουγα (ákugha = I was listening).
Wanting is a state, managing it is one-off: ήθελα, αλλά δεν μπόρεσα (íthela, allá dhen bóresa = I wanted to, but I couldn't).
Περίμενα μισή ώρα (perímena misí óra) can mean 'I waited' or 'I was waiting' half an hour – the two past forms coincide here, so context decides.
Για (ya) usually means 'for', but after speech verbs it's 'about': μιλούσαμε για σένα (milúsame ya séna = we were talking about you).
Background weather usually takes the ongoing past: έκανε κρύο (ékane krío = it was cold); the one-off event gets the simple past – βγήκαμε (vyíkame = we went out).
Two habits, two ongoing pasts: δούλευα (dhúleva = I worked), ξυπνούσα (ksipnúsa = I used to wake up).
Χτυπάω (khtipáo = knock, ring) covers phones and doors alike: χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο (khtípise to tiléfono = the phone rang).
Ενώ (enó = while) pairs with the ongoing past: ενώ μαγείρευα (enó mayíreva = while I was cooking).
Μόλις (mólis = as soon as) takes the one-off past: μόλις μπήκα (mólis bíka = as soon as I came in).
Θα (tha) plus the one-shot verb form makes a single future act: θα ξυπνήσω (tha ksipníso = I'll wake up).
Θα περάσω από την τράπεζα (tha peráso apó tin trápeza) is literally 'I'll pass from the bank': περνάω από (pernáo apó) is how you say 'stop by'.
Κατά τις οχτώ (katá tis okhtó = around eight) – κατά makes a clock time approximate.
Θα κοιμηθώ (tha kimithó = I'll sleep) – the ending looks like the done-to-you form, but this verb only comes in that shape.
Δεν θα βγω (dhen tha vgho = I won't go out) – 'not' goes first, before the future word θα, never between it and the verb.
The short 'you' word sits inside the future phrase: θα σε πάρω (tha se páro = I'll call you) – σε (se) slots between θα (tha) and the verb.
Θα σου πω (tha su po = I'll tell you) – the little word for 'you' slips in between the future word θα (tha) and the verb.
Θα σε περιμένω (tha se periméno = I'll wait for you) – Greek drops the 'for': you wait someone, directly.
Θα τα πούμε (tha ta púme = we'll talk, lit. we'll say them) – a standard goodbye.
Greek asks for forgiveness rather than 'apologizing': θα της ζητήσω συγγνώμη (tha tis zitíso sighnómi = I'll ask her for forgiveness).
Θα μπορέσω (tha boréso = I'll manage to) – one occasion, vs μπορώ (boró = I can) in general.
Μόλις (mólis = as soon as) takes the plain one-shot form with no θα: μόλις φτάσω (mólis ftáso = as soon as I arrive).
Στης μαμάς (stis mamás = at mom's) – the word σπίτι (spíti = house) is understood.
Θα (tha) with the ongoing verb form stretches the future out: θα κοιμάμαι (tha kimáme = I'll be sleeping).
Κάνουμε τραπέζι (kánume trapézi = we host a meal, lit. we make a table) – that's how you invite people over for dinner.
Του χρόνου (tu khrónu = next year, lit. of the year).
Κλείνω (klíno) literally means 'close' – Greek closes what it books: θα κλείσω τα εισιτήρια (tha klíso ta isitíria = I'll book the tickets). Tables too.
Κάθε πρωί (káthe proí = every morning) means repeated, so the future keeps the ongoing form: θα κολυμπάμε (tha kolimbáme = we'll be swimming).
